description: Desarrollador: Android/React Native, Node y análisis de datos.
summary:
In the Andes of Huánuco, Peru, there is one rain-fed growing season a year. A farmer chooses what to sow once, and if the rains arrive late or the frost comes early, the year is lost. NASA has measured that rainfall for decades, but the data lives in global grids, in English, behind an internet connection the field does not have.

Yachay Allpa ("knowledge of the land" in Quechua) turns NASA POWER, GPM IMERG and GIBS into a single decision for the 11 provinces of Huánuco: what to plant, when, and why. It compares three crop-rotation strategies — keeping the current one, an Andean rotation, and a water-saving option — and shows the evidence behind each: expected harvest, water gap in litres per m², and frost nights out of 100, for that exact field. On a real field at 1,900 m, keeping the current rotation returns 61 % of what the land could give, while two alternatives reach 74 % — same field, same NASA data.

All heavy computation is precomputed, so the recommendation runs on the phone with no signal, in Spanish and Quechua, with no account or sign-up.
details:
What it does

Yachay Allpa answers one question for a smallholder farmer in Huánuco, Peru: what to sow, and when. It gives a verdict — plant this week, wait for the rain, wait for the frost to pass, or rest the land — never an unresolved list of options. Alongside the verdict it compares three rotation strategies (keep as is, Andean rotation, water-saving) with the expected harvest of each, what it gains and what it risks.

How it works

Heavy data processing runs on a small server once a day; the decision itself runs on the phone, so a farmer with no coverage still gets an answer. Season packs ship inside the APK, the daily update is 1.2 KB per zone, and the relief map is bundled. Once the data is on the device, a recommendation costs zero bytes.

The method

The chain from measured rain to expected harvest is deliberately traceable. Effective rain follows the USDA SCS method as applied in FAO CROPWAT. Crop demand follows FAO-56 (ETc = Kc x ETo), with ETo corrected from the NASA cell altitude to the field altitude at -6.5 C/km. Expected harvest follows FAO-33 (Doorenbos and Kassam, 1979), averaged over 15 seasons rather than a single year. The onset of sowing uses the 25 mm over 10 days criterion with no 7-day dry spell in the following 30 (Lodoun et al., 2013), or 20 mm in 3 days (Sivakumar, 1988) before the season starts. Frost is counted as nights below the crop's tolerance, with minimum temperature corrected to field altitude. The verdict shown to the farmer is the worst of three gauges — score, water and frost — so the app can never report a good option while the water balance says otherwise.

Tools

Decision engine in plain Java 11 with no Android dependency, so it is fully testable. Android app in Kotlin with Jetpack Compose, in Spanish and Quechua. Daily data job in Node.js. Helper scripts in Python. Season packs are signed with ECDSA P-256 and verified on the device, so a tampered pack is rejected before it can reach a farmer's decision. Apache 2.0 licence, with every dataset, formula and font cited in SOURCES.md.

Impact and what we considered

Repeating the same crop season after season is the common fallback in the region, and it is the costly one. The gap we measured on one field — 61 percent against 74 percent of attainable yield — is a year of food and income, obtained from data that already exists and was already paid for. We treated three constraints as hard requirements rather than features: it must work with no signal, it must speak Spanish and Quechua, and it must not collect anything about the farmer. GPS stays on the device, and only the fixed centre of the NASA grid cell is ever used to fetch data. We also handled a known data pitfall explicitly: NASA POWER fills its most recent months with GEOS-IT, which is biased wet, so the pipeline, the server and the phone all cut the series at the last reliable month and use IMERG for anything newer.

Limitations

The tool supports the farmer, it does not replace them. Crop coefficients, altitude ranges and sowing months are FAO and INIA reference values, not measured in Huánuco; an agronomist needs to tune them to local fields.
